list.listitem: The diagnosis of Meniere's disease requires more than one episode of vertigo, hearing loss documented by audiometry, and tinnitus. C
None of the commonly used therapies (diuretics, antihistamines) has been shown to work better than placebo. B
Small studies show benefit for booklet based self management of symptoms, and intratympanic steroids or gentamicin. B
With time, episodes of vertigo typically decrease or diminish. However, hearing loss worsens and often becomes bilateral. C

background.definition: Meniere's disease is a clinical syndrome characterized by vertigo, tinnitus, fluctuating hearing impairment, and a sensation of pressure or fullness in the ear.

list.listitem: Precise incidence is unknown because of nonstandard diagnostic criteria.
Estimated prevalence is 1 in 1000 in United Kingdom.
Although the pathologic lesion of Meniere's disease is known, it is unclear why excess fluid builds up in the endolymphatic spaces of the inner ear.
Several theories exist to explain why this occurs, but all are unproved.
The classic pathologic lesion is endolymphatic hydrops: raised endolymph pressure in the membranous labyrinth.
It can be definitively diagnosed only by pathologic analysis of the temporal bone postmortem.
Patients typically present with vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss. All three are required for the diagnosis. C
Consider MRI with and without contrast for the patient presenting with sensorineural hearing loss and acute or intermittent vertigo.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Typically progressive hearing loss, not fluctuating; usually imbalance, not true vertigo
Nystagmus during an attack more severe and longer lasting
Shorter duration, rarely objective hearing loss
Hearing loss does not persist; headache during or after episode; may have no ear symptoms

list.listitem: The American Academy of Otolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery requires the following for a definite diagnosis of Meniere's disease: (1) at least two spontaneous episodes of rotational vertigo lasting for at least 20 minutes, (2) audiometrically confirmed sensorineural hearing loss, (3) tinnitus or aural fullness during episodes, and (4) exclusion of other possible causes of vertigo.
Presentation differs based on stage of disease, see .

Vertigo may be associated with nausea and vomiting, pallor, and sweating. Loss of consciousness does not occur. Two-thirds of patients will have more than 12 vertigo attacks per year, and in most the attacks will last for less than 1 day.
Hearing loss is sensorineural, characteristically affecting the lower frequencies. The hearing loss may progress over time, affecting both ears and leading to permanent loss at all frequencies.
The aura of fullness or pressure in the ear can last from 20 minutes to several hours and often precedes the vertigo.
Tinnitus is usually of low pitch.
Audiometry is required to confirm the diagnosis of Meniere's disease.

MRI with and without contrast is recommended to rule out infectious or neoplastic causes of the symptoms in patients presenting with sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo. CT of head without contrast is an option if cholesteatoma is suspected.
Delayed acquisition of post-gadolinium MRI can identify endolymphatic hydrops in patient's with suspected Meniere's disease.
Suspect Meniere's disease in patients presenting with a complaint of hearing loss, tinnitus, and/or vertigo.
Order audiometry to confirm hearing loss.
Commonly used treatments include dietary restrictions; drug therapy with diuretics, antiemetics, or antihistamines; and destructive and conservative surgical procedures. C
No drug therapy has been shown in well-designed clinical trials to affect the clinical course of the disease and prevent the progressive hearing loss. B
Intratympanic gentamicin injection appears to be an effective treatment for vertigo in Meniere's disease but may increase risk of hearing loss.
The most common surgical procedure is endolymphatic sac surgery, but it has not been shown to be better than sham surgery. B
No drug treatment has been proved in well-designed, adequately powered studies to modify the clinical course of the disease or prevent the progressive hearing loss.
Drug therapy has been associated with a significant placebo effect; because the disorder relapses and remits, the effect of treatment is difficult to assess.

A Cochrane review identified 5 RCTs with a total of only 137 participants comparing intratympanic gentamicin with placebo. They noted a possible improvement in vertigo with gentamicin, although the certainty of evidence was judged to be very low.

A Cochrane review of 10 randomized placebo-controlled trials with 952 participants found insufficient evidence to support use of diuretics for vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, or aural fullness in patients with clearly defined Meniere's disease. Two large RCTs remain unpublished raising the concern for publication bias.

A systematic review of randomized controlled studies of betahistine vs. placebo concluded that there is insufficient evidence to say whether betahistine has any effect on Meniere's disease.Betahistine is widely available outside the United States but is not approved for sale in the US.
Other classes of medications that are used (without supporting evidence) for treatment include antiemetics, anxiolytics, and antihistamines.
There is also no evidence that tricyclic antidepressants or SSRIs improve symptoms of tinnitus.

The most commonly used initial procedure is a conservative one, endolymphatic sac surgery. However, it has not been shown to be better than sham surgery. Authors of a Cochrane review also found insufficient evidence to conclude whether is a benefit of endolymphatic surgery in Meniere's disease.
Labyrinthinectomy and other destructive procedures destroy vestibular function and hearing, and are generally reserved for patients who already have nonfunctioning hearing in the affected ear.
Intratympanic instillation of gentamicin may be effective for vertigo complaints but carries a risk of hearing loss. Overall the evidence for intratympanic gentamicin is uncertain.
Intratympanic gentamicin injection may be an option but is not clearly superior to intratympanic steroid injection.

Two small randomized double blind placebo controlled trials showed improvement in vertigo symptoms with a Meniett low pressure pulse generator device. It provides positive pressure into the ear canal.
A Cochrane review concluded that the evidence for intratympanic steroids is uncertain.
There is insufficient evidence to know if micropressure therapy is safe in refractory disease (NICE guideline April 2012).
Dietary restrictions on salt, caffeine, alcohol, and tobacco have been recommended based on anecdotes but have not been evaluated in randomized trials.
A randomized controlled trial demonstrated that self-management booklets offer an inexpensive and easily disseminated means of helping people with Meniere's disease to cope with dizziness.
A Cochrane review concluded that the current evidence does not support positive pressure devices, based on 3 small RCTs.
Depression is common in patients with Meniere's disease. Consider screening and appropriate treatment.
Guidance for the management of drop attacks in Meniere's disease is limited.
Remissions and exacerbations are typical of Meniere's disease. C
With time, vertigo attacks often diminish or disappear, although almost half of patients will have bilateral symptoms after 20 years of followup. B
Hearing loss progressively worsens over time. C

tr.td: Stage I. The predominant symptom is vertigo. Between the attacks, hearing reverts to normal. Examination of the patient between attacks is normal.

Stage II. As the disease advances, the hearing loss becomes established but still fluctuates. The episodes of vertigo reach their worst severity and then become less severe. The period of time between episodes is highly variable, but often lasts several months.
Stage III. The hearing loss no longer fluctuates and progressively worsens. The major disability is deafness. The episodes of vertigo decrease and disappear, although the patient may be unsteady.
